title: Cellar Safety & CO2 Awareness
blurb: The hazards of a cellar, above all CO2: what the gas alarm means, why you never go in, and safe everyday habits.
siteNotes: Where the cellar gas alarm is, what it sounds like and who to tell when it goes off
The correct procedure for changing gas cylinders here, and who is trained to do it
Where the cellar vents are and the rule for keeping the cellar door open or closed
Who to report a gas leak or damaged cylinder to, and the out-of-hours contact
legalNotes: From BHB-10MT-28. CO2 as an asphyxiant in confined cellar spaces: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, and HSE guidance on dispense gases in pubs and cellars. Manual handling and slips: Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992 and general duties.

CHECK: the trainer does not say the venue's alarm must be tested and maintained, or that cylinder changes need trained, authorised staff. Confirm the venue's CO2 detector is installed, tested and serviced on a schedule, and who is authorised to change cylinders.

CHECK: the trainer treats "if the alarm sounds, do not go in" as the rule. Confirm the venue has a written emergency procedure for a collapsed person in the cellar (call 999, do not enter to rescue) and that staff have been told it.

cards.title: Cellar Safety & CO2 Awareness
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- explain why CO2 in a cellar is dangerous
- respond correctly to the gas alarm
- keep the cellar ventilated, clear and safe

cards.title: Small, cold, full of hazards
cards.body: The cellar is the engine room of the bar, but it packs several hazards into one small, cold space: heavy kegs, wet floors and, the big one, gas.

items.title: Wet floors
items.text: Slip hazard in a cold space

items.title: Steps and drops
items.text: Take care going up and down

cards.title: CO2 is invisible
cards.body:
The CO2 and mixed gas used to dispense drinks is invisible and has no real smell. In a confined space it can build up and displace oxygen, which can cause someone to collapse or even suffocate.
> It is not something to be casual about.

cards.title: If it sounds, do not go in
cards.body: Know where the cellar gas alarm is and what it sounds like. Treat it deadly seriously. Never try to "just nip in" to grab something while an alarm is sounding.

items.title: Report it
items.text: Straight away, so it is dealt with safely

cards.title: Air and gas cylinders
cards.body: Good ventilation is essential. Never block vents or prop the cellar in a way that stops air moving. Change gas cylinders carefully, following the correct procedure, and secure them so they cannot fall.

left.title: Do
items: Secure cylinders so they cannot fall

cards.title: Leaks and everyday habits
cards.body: If you smell or suspect a gas leak, or a cylinder is damaged, treat it as urgent and report it. The rest is good housekeeping.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- CO2 is invisible, has no real smell and can displace oxygen.
- Alarm sounding: do not go in. Stay out, keep others away and report it.
- Never block vents. Secure gas cylinders.
- Suspected leak or damaged cylinder: urgent, report it.
- Keep floors clear and dry and handle kegs properly.

cards.q: CO2 in a confined cellar can displace oxygen and cause someone to collapse.
cards.why: In a confined space CO2 can displace oxygen, and someone can collapse or even suffocate.

cards.q: If the CO2 gas alarm sounds, what should you do?
options: Go in quickly and turn off the cylinders
Prop the door open and wait inside
Silence the alarm and carry on working
Stay out, keep others away and report it
cards.why: Do not go in. Get out or stay out, keep others away and report it immediately.

cards.q: CO2 gas is easy to spot because it's brightly coloured and smells strong.
cards.why: CO2 is invisible and has no real smell, which is why the alarm matters.
Good ventilation is essential. Never block vents or stop air moving.

cards.q: It's fine to nip into the cellar quickly even if the alarm is sounding.
cards.why: Never try to "just nip in" while an alarm is sounding. Stay out and report it.
Change cylinders carefully following the correct procedure and secure them so they cannot fall.

cards.q: Which is a hazard in the cellar other than gas?
cards.why: The cellar combines heavy kegs, wet floors and steps and drops, as well as gas.

cards.q: Good ventilation is essential in a cellar.
cards.why: Ventilation stops gas building up, so never block vents.

cards.q: You suspect a gas leak or spot a damaged cylinder. You should…
options: Ignore it unless it gets worse
Fix it yourself if it is small
Wait and see if it gets worse
Treat it as urgent and report it
cards.why: A suspected leak or a damaged cylinder is urgent. Report it.

cards.q: Keeping cellar floors clear and dry helps prevent slips.
cards.why: Clear, dry floors prevent slips, one of the cellar's everyday hazards.
